Fuzzy Logic in Modern AI
Where it fits alongside Machine Learning and Neural Networks
1965
Lotfi Zadeh publishes
“Fuzzy Sets”
1974
First fuzzy controller
(steam engine, Mamdani)
Today
Neuro-fuzzy systems,
explainable control
Presented By:- Sezal (24BAI70653)
                            Minazpreet (24BAI70630)

THE CORE IDEA
Crisp sets say yes or no. Fuzzy sets say how much.
Classical (crisp) logic
IF temp > 28 THEN hot
27.9°C → not hot (0)
28.1°C → hot (1)
Fuzzy logic
A membership function μ(x) maps every value to a degree in [0, 1].
At 27°C:   μ_Warm = 0.6   and   μ_Hot = 0.4
The reading belongs to both sets — no knife-edge, no jitter when the sensor wobbles by 0.2°.
Read the chart at 27°C: the amber curve sits at 0.6, the red at 0.4 — the sum of memberships need not be 1, but here it is.

HOW A FUZZY SYSTEM IS BUILT
Four stages: numbers in, rules in the middle, numbers out
Crisp input
T = 27°C
H = 65%
Fuzzification
Convert each reading
into memberships
Inference engine
Fire every rule,
take min / max
Defuzzification
Collapse the fuzzy
output to one number
Crisp output
Fan speed
= 82%
Rule base  (written by a human expert)
IF temp is Warm AND humidity is High
THEN fan is High
1
No training data is required.
Knowledge enters as sentences, not as a labelled dataset.
2
Every decision is traceable.
You can name the rules that fired and by how much.
3
Cost: the rules are hand-made.
Team membership shapes by hand does not scale.

WORKED EXAMPLE  ·  AIR-CONDITIONER CONTROLLER
Step 1 — fuzzify the sensors, then fire the rules
Sensor readings
T = 27°C        H = 65%
Temperature — triangles (15,20,25) (20,25,30) (25,30,35)
μ_Cool(27) = 0
μ_Warm(27) = (30 − 27) / 5 = 0.6
μ_Hot(27)  = (27 − 25) / 5 = 0.4
Humidity — triangles (0,25,50) (25,50,75) (50,75,100)
μ_Low(65)  = 0
μ_Med(65)  = (75 − 65) / 25 = 0.4
μ_High(65) = (65 − 50) / 25 = 0.6
Two crisp numbers have become four non-zero memberships.
Step 2 — firing strength of each rule,  α = min(antecedents)
IF temp is
AND humidity is
THEN fan is
firing strength α
R1
Warm
Medium
Medium (55%)
min(0.6, 0.4) = 0.4
R2
Warm
High
High (85%)
min(0.6, 0.6) = 0.6
R3
Hot
Medium
High (85%)
min(0.4, 0.4) = 0.4
R4
Hot
High
Max (100%)
min(0.4, 0.6) = 0.4
Why min?  AND in fuzzy logic is the weakest link — a rule can only be as true as its least-satisfied condition. (OR would use max.) All four rules fire at once; classical logic would have picked exactly one.

WORKED EXAMPLE  ·  CONTINUED
Step 3 — aggregate the fired rules into one fan speed
Each output set is represented by its centre: Medium = 55, High = 85, Max = 100. Weighted-average defuzzification then takes the centre of gravity.
Fan speed  =  Σ αᵢ zᵢ  /  Σ αᵢ
numerator  = 0.4(55) + 0.6(85) + 0.4(85) + 0.4(100)
           = 22 + 51 + 34 + 40  =  147
denominator = 0.4 + 0.6 + 0.4 + 0.4  =  1.8
fan speed  = 147 / 1.8  =  81.7
Mamdani variant: aggregate the two High rules with max(0.6, 0.4) = 0.6 first, and the centroid gives 80.7 — the same control decision.
≈ 82%
fan speed. Nudge the room to 26°C and the output glides to roughly 74% — no step, no relay chatter, no oscillation around a threshold.

WHERE IT FITS
Where does the knowledge come from?
Fuzzy Logic
Classical ML
Neural Networks
Knowledge source
Human expert writes the rules
Features + labelled examples
Raw data, learned end-to-end
Data needed
None to start
Thousands of rows
Tens of thousands upward
Transparency
Full — you can read every rule
Moderate — weights, splits
Low — millions of parameters
Handles vagueness
By design: “warm”, “mildly risky”
Only as probability
Implicit in the representation
Adapts on its own
No — rules are static
Yes — by retraining
Yes — by gradient descent
Strongest at
Control, safety limits, small expert domains
Tabular prediction, ranking
Vision, language, speech
Rule of thumb for the exam: fuzzy logic encodes knowledge you already have; machine learning extracts knowledge you don't.

THE INTERESTING PART
Modern systems combine them rather than choose
ANFIS
Neuro-fuzzy inference
A fuzzy rule base laid out as a 5-layer network, so membership-function parameters are trained by gradient descent.
You keep readable rules and still learn from data.
FCM
Fuzzy c-means clustering
Each point gets a membership in every cluster instead of one hard label — the soft cousin of k-means.
Used in MRI tissue segmentation.
XAI
Fuzzy explanation layers
A rule base is fitted on top of a trained network so its behaviour can be described in words.
Turns “0.87 risk” into “high BP AND high glucose”.
Inside ANFIS

output
layers 4–5 trained by least squares, layers 1–2 by backpropagation

WHERE YOU ALREADY MEET IT
Quietly running in hardware you use every week
Washing machines
Load, fabric and dirt level set the cycle time — Panasonic and Hitachi shipped this from the late 1980s.
Camera autofocus
Contrast and motion cues are blended to decide how far to drive the lens.
Sendai subway
Fuzzy braking since 1987; passengers report noticeably smoother stops than manual driving.
Anti-lock braking
Slip ratio and wheel deceleration are graded, not thresholded.
Medical decision aids
Symptom severity is naturally vague; rules stay readable for clinicians.
Traffic signal control
Queue length and waiting time in degrees rather than fixed cut-offs.
Takeaway
Fuzzy logic is not an older rival of machine learning — it is the part of AI that handles vagueness in human language and keeps decisions readable. Where data is scarce, rules are known, or an auditor must follow the reasoning, it still wins; everywhere else it now works as a layer inside a learning system.
